teaser: He worked for ten months, drew this face, and vanished. Nobody is sure who he was.
review_notes:
Career: about 10 months (5th month 1794 to 1st month 1795), over 140 designs; first group of 28 bust portraits.
Play: Koi nyobo somewake tazuna, Kawarazaki theater, 5th month 1794; Edobei robs the servant Ippei (played by Ichikawa Omezo, companion print).
Contemporary comment that he drew too truthfully and did not last: paraphrased from the Ukiyo-e ruiko (Ota Nanpo).
Identity as Noh actor Saito Jurobei: leading theory, not proven.
Julius Kurth's 1910 book and the comparison with Rembrandt and Velazquez.
Crest character read as 'oni' (demon) from the image.
The image matches the listed print (catalog match was 'fulltext').

lesson.text: Ten months. That is the entire career of the artist who signed himself Sharaku. His first prints went on sale in Edo in the summer of 1794. By early 1795 he had designed more than 140, and then he stopped. No farewell, no later work, no grave anyone can point to with certainty.

This sheet comes from his opening burst: 28 portraits of kabuki actors, all issued at once. Kabuki was the popular theater of the city, loud, stylized and played entirely by men. Fans bought prints of their favorite stars the way people later bought posters.

The man here is the actor Otani Oniji III. He is playing Edobei, a hired thug, in a play staged in the fifth month of 1794. In the scene, Edobei jumps a servant on the road to steal his master's money. Sharaku freezes him one heartbeat before the grab.

lesson.title: A face at full stretch
lesson.text: Kabuki actors hold a frozen pose at the peak of a scene, called a mie. Follow it from top to bottom.

spots.title: The eyes
spots.text: Pupils pushed toward the nose, ringed with red makeup, under eyebrows like two brushstrokes. Crossing the eyes was part of the stage pose, a sign of fury held still.

spots.title: The mouth
spots.text: A long downturned line, clamped shut. The jaw juts forward past the nose. Sharaku stretches the real proportions to get the sneer.

spots.title: The hands
spots.text: Ten spread fingers burst out of the kimono. They are too small for the head and oddly jointed, yet they are what you remember: grasping, twitching, ready.

lesson.text: Those hands have annoyed and fascinated people for two centuries. Are they clumsy, or deliberate? Either way, the mismatch works. A huge head and small clawing hands make the body feel squeezed forward, like a spring about to release.
The dark background is not plain ink. It was coated with ground mica mixed into black, so the surface glinted like dull metal behind the pale face. It was a costly finish for a picture of a villain.
Other artists flattered actors. Sharaku drew the aging man under the makeup: the big nose, the heavy chin, the effort. He even kept track of who was who, in a way a theater fan would catch at once.
The actor's name, Oniji, begins with the word “oni”, which means demon. That character is written somewhere on his costume. Can you spot it?

spots.title: The actor's crest
spots.text: A pale disc on the striped sleeve carries the character for “demon”. It is the actor's personal crest, not the character's. The print shows a role and names the star at once.

lesson.text: A Sharaku portrait shows two people in one face: the character on stage and the particular actor straining to play him.

That honesty may have been his undoing. A writer of the period noted that Sharaku tried so hard to draw actors truthfully that he showed them as they should not be seen, and so he did not last. Stars, and the fans who adored them, did not want their idols with flaws.

The most widely accepted guess about his identity is that he was Saito Jurobei, an actor of Noh, the slow, masked theater of the nobility, employed by a provincial lord. If so, he was a stage professional watching a rival stage.

One man clearly believed in him. The publisher Tsutaya Juzaburo, who had already backed Utamaro, paid for mica backgrounds and released all 28 portraits together, a huge bet on an unknown name. Both men left their marks on the sheet.

spots.title: The signature
spots.text: Written top to bottom: “Toshusai Sharaku drew this”. A pen name, and the only biography he left.

spots.title: Two seals
spots.text: The ivy leaf under a peak is the publisher Tsutaya's mark. The small round stamp above it is the censor's approval, required on every print sold.

spots.title: The hair
spots.text: Hundreds of hair-thin white lines along the edge of the topknot. Each is a sliver of wood the carver cut away, working from Sharaku's drawing.

spots.title: The red under-robe
spots.text: A flash of red beneath black and stripes. On it you can make out the sketchy outline of a pattern, drawn in just a few lines.

spots.title: The mica ground
spots.text: Where the dark coating is worn, the surface turns gray and patchy. On a fresh impression it would have been an even, sparkling field.

lesson.text: In Japan he was largely forgotten for a century. His reputation came back from abroad: in 1910 a German scholar, Julius Kurth, published a book ranking him among the great portraitists of the world. Japanese collectors looked again, and by then many of the finest impressions were already in Western museums.

So the question stays open. An unknown appears, makes some of the most intense faces in Japanese art, and disappears before a year is out. Was he pushed out by poor sales, called back to his day job, or simply finished?

quiz.question: How long did Sharaku's career as a print designer last?
Who is Edobei in the play?
options: A hired thug about to rob someone
quiz.explanation: He ambushes a servant to steal money.

quiz.question: What does the crest on the sleeve identify?
quiz.explanation: It carries the character “oni”, the first part of the actor's name.

quiz.question: What gave the dark background its glint?
quiz.explanation: Ground mica was mixed into the black coating.

quiz.question: What is a mie?
options: A frozen pose at the peak of a scene
quiz.explanation: Kabuki actors hold the pose, often crossing their eyes.

facts.text: Sharaku's portraits were designed to flatter the actors.
facts.explanation: He drew their real features, which may have cost him his audience.

facts.text: The same publisher backed both Utamaro and Sharaku.
facts.explanation: Tsutaya Juzaburo, whose ivy-leaf seal is on the sheet.

facts.text: Kabuki in Sharaku's time was performed only by men.
facts.explanation: All roles, including women's, were played by male actors.
